This is stated in a press release published on the company's official LinkedIn page . Making a reference to Grigoryan's work experience in the highest levels of public administration, PMCG notes that his career includes the areas of strategic management, diplomacy, institutional reforms, crisis management, and regional security. According to the press release, the newly appointed senior advisor is already actively engaged in the work of PMCG; in particular, in the process of assessing the feasibility of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) infrastructure program. Armen Grigoryan held the position of Secretary of the Security Council of Armenia from 2018 to 2026. By the decision of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, however, Grigoryan was relieved of this post in August of this year, declining to remain in the executive branch for another position offered by the premier. Grigoryan briefly served as the Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs of Armenia in 2021. PMCG is an international development advisory network that aims to ensure the progress of transition and developing countries. The company operates in the US, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia, Uzbekistan, Poland, and Ireland, collaborating with local governments, international organizations, and the private sector. The organization, represented in Armenia by PMCG Armenia LLC, specializes in implementing structural reforms aimed at socioeconomic prosperity and institutional capacity development. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/Shutterstock New Jersey New Jersey governor calls on lieutenant governor to resign after ethics investigation Mikie Sherrill says Dale Caldwell ‘engaged in serious, repeated violations’ involving staffers and gifts Associated Press Thu 24 Sep 2026 21.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New Jersey’s governor on Thursday called on the state’s lieutenant governor, Dale Caldwell, to resign by Friday after a law firm hired by her office concluded he violated the state’s ethics and discrimination rules. The report published Wednesday found that Caldwell violated the state’s policy prohibiting discrimination in the workplace. It said he made an advance toward a staffer’s friend and when he was rebuffed, he told the staffer: “You young women are looking for young sperm.” “The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office,” Mikie Sherrill, the governor, said in a statement. Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the allegations, calling the investigation a one-sided operation that did not include necessary due process. “The Lieutenant Governor was not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations,” he said in a statement. The report also accused Caldwell of breaking the state’s ethics rules by trying to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating and by bringing his personal guests to ticketed events without paying for them. “Where a sponsor waives admission to an event for an official’s family member, friend, or date, the value of that admission is an impermissible benefit to the official,” the report said. Sherrill, a Democrat, said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses” continued even with multiple warnings and trainings. She called his resignation “in the best interest of New Jersey residents”. “These violations substantiated in the investigation reflect a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this Administration,” she said. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Reuters Brexit Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms Ken McCallum says Kremlin attempted to influence vote through social media and TV reports but had little impact Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.15 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham , who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions . Other studies have reported on a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeting about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers active have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000 . Burnham had first returned to the issue on Sunday, during a podcast interview, though at first it was unclear whether the prime minister had been given new intelligence on a topic that had largely been considered forgotten. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” said the prime minister, implying he had a discussion or briefing on the issue. A day later, however, he backed off when challenged by the Conservatives on whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate, and he did not supply any additional information in the Commons. On Tuesday Downing Street said it had been confirmed that Russia interfered in the 2019 general election and it was “inconceivable that they didn’t in 2016”. But the prime minister’s spokesperson added: “We don’t believe it was successful in the British referendum in 2016.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion McCallum said it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was the subject of controversy for several more days. “It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us,” he said. Continued attention gave the impression that Kremlin disinformation attempts were more successful than they actually were, the MI5 chief added. “I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front-page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey,” he said. Janet Leigh and her daughter Jamie Lee Curtis in 1998 On October 3, 2004, the Psycho legend died of vasculitis - an inflammation of the blood vessels - at the age of 77. Taking to Instagram on Saturday (03.10.26), Jamie, 67, shared a black-and-white shot of Janet playing in a bubble bath, with the caption: "Long time gone this day. Love and misses to my mother." Fans took to the post's comments section to pay tribute to the Halloween icon's mom, as one penned: "That's so sweet. I was just watching Psycho today. What a beautiful lady..... (sic)" A second supporter typed: "Just finished her incredible memoir. Remarkable, talented woman." And a third follower wrote: "A true legend of cinema, like yourself and your father." Janet was married to the late actor Tony Curtis from 1951 until 1962. The couple welcomed their daughters, actresses Kelly Curtis and Jamie, in 1956 and 1958, respectively. Kelly, who starred alongside her parents in the 1958's action-adventure film, The Vikings, and Jamie in the 1983 comedy-drama movie, Trading Places, died of natural causes on May 30 at the age of 69. Jamie took to Instagram to pay tribute by sharing a black-and-white photo of Kelly, with the caption: "A warm aloha to my older sister, Kelly Lee Curtis. She passed away this morning. In her home. In nature. At peace. "She was my first friend and lifelong confidant. She was jaw droppingly beautiful, and a talented actress. "She played a mean game of hearts, collected turtles, loved her family, nature, music, thrifting, travel, Facebook, and Pokemon Go. She was proud of her Danish roots and Hungarian Jewish ancestry and was a devoted American patriot. "She will be remembered for her loving generosity, fierce opinions, endless curiosity, unique style, and her powdered, almond, crescent cookies at Christmas, hence her name, Auntie Cookie. "Kelly always signed off any message or fare thee well with a Hungarian blessing… "Isten Veled, God is with you. (sic)" The sisters both faced accusations of nepotism early in their acting careers. However, Jamie pushed back against accusations that she is a so-called nepo baby earlier this year. In January, the Freaky Friday alum told CBS News: "I guarantee you, the fact that my mother was in Psycho was a determining factor that maybe that will get them a little extra publicity. "Now, did it get me to that final two? No, my auditions got me to the final two." Tagged in Jamie Lee Curtis Tony Curtis Janet Leigh Competitions Hot Articles Most Popular

Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters View image in fullscreen US President Donald Trump might still lash out at Europe even while facing defeat at home. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters This Is Europe World news Is the US blue wave a turning point for Europe, too? Far-right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for Trump’s betrayal. But the midterms also showed that democracy can fight back Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Katherine Butler , associate editor, Europe Wed 11 Nov 2026 10.40 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 10.42 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “I s Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone. The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has been met with understandable relief in European capitals. In the short term however, the worst for Europe is not over. Trump didn’t need congressional approval, after all, to unleash a trade war on his supposed European allies, threaten to invade Greenland, try to stitch up Ukraine or go to war with Iran, an act that has inflated fuel and food prices disastrously. Hemmed in now on domestic policy, the US president may, many European leaders fear, use his extensive foreign policy powers to become even more confrontational on the world stage. Europe, warned Nathalie Tocci , is exactly where Trump will lash out. “Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.” The lashing out could come in the form of new tariff chaos. As the humiliated Maga figurehead (one Washington expert likened the movement now to “a cornered ferret”), Trump could veto aid for Ukraine and thwart Kyiv’s access to defence technology. Paul Taylor sketched a fearful scenario in which he could even attempt a carve-up of eastern Europe in the so-called “big, beautiful deal” for Ukraine that he says he is working on with Russia. The omens for Europe were poor as US-mediated talks opened in Abu Dhabi , with delegates from Germany, France, the UK and the EU, literally sidelined. Nor can Europe rely on the new intake of congressional Democrats to challenge Trump on its behalf, Blanche Leridon of the Institut Montaigne thinktank in Paris, tells me. “We have to be clear-sighted that the Democrats’ priority in Congress won’t be to re-establish a more harmonious relationship with Europe. Their foreign policy is, at this point, difficult to decipher. There isn’t a single, consistent position between the more progressive and centrist factions when it comes to either Europe or Ukraine specifically.” We can’t even assume that nationalist populist parties, encouraged by Trump to destroy the EU from the inside, will suffer by their association with him. True, in central and eastern Europe, where the Maga spirit was heavily promoted by Viktor Orbán, some incumbents may have to perform a pivot. Poland’s conservative president Karol Nawrocki , who is backed by the opposition Eurosceptic Law and Justice party and has vaunted his proximity to Trump, is now facing awkward questions. And in Czechia, which has one of the most pro-Maga governments in Europe , populist PM Andrej Babiš and his far-right coalition partners, the Motorists party, have faced a wave of grassroots protests lately. In Italy meanwhile, the far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni played up tensions with Trump months ago, a strategic move to allay the concerns of voters, the majority of whom despise him. But in countries where populists have not yet been in government and are polling at record levels, Trump’s humiliation may not matter to voters, even if their grievances – such as stagnant pay, inflation and lack of affordable housing – are often driven by global forces. “It would be wrong to conclude that national-populist and reactionary forces are in retreat everywhere in the west,” Leridon says. “The Democrats won in the US because people were fed up with Trump, in Serbia , [Aleksandar] Vučić was overthrown after 14 years, but in countries where populist political forces are not in power, but on the verge of gaining it, the calculation is different.” In France, Marine Le Pen is still leading in the polls, six months ahead of a presidential election being fought on cost-of-living issues. Her far-right National Rally party identified Trump as a liability some time ago. “Le Pen and [Jordan] Bardella understood perfectly the radioactive effect the US president could have on them as politicians claiming to defend French national interests. Above all, they recoiled from the corrosive impact of Trump’s policies on purchasing power in France, whether via trade tariffs or the war in Iran,” Leridon says. In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, had also distanced the party from Trump in response to tariffs and Greenland. Weidel now blames Trump’s defeat on broken promises about going to war with Iran. A critical test for Europe’s political direction is looming in Spain. Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez, who called a snap election for 29 November , welcomed Trump’s defeat as a straw in the wind for the revival of progressive forces. But amid public outcry over housing and wages (the cause of Wednesday’s general strike ), the momentum is with the opposition rightwing Popular Party (PP) – which could coalesce with the far-right Vox. If this happens, it will be the first time a far-right party enters government in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975. Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, dismissed any suggestion of an ideological connection with Trump’s Republicans. “We are in Spain, not in Michigan,” he said after the midterms. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion A yearning for generational change View image in fullscreen The youth movement in Serbia toppled a government. Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters And yet, longer term, the broader, more hopeful lesson from across the Atlantic could be that after years of global backsliding liberal democracy is not dead. “If Europe can celebrate an essential point, it is that American democracy is alive and was the big winner of these elections,” Leridon says. Could this even, as Alexander Hurst asked , be a “democratic spring” – one that began in Budapest in April with Orbán’s defeat? Julian Borger unpacked how a sequence of four pivotal elections this year, in Hungary, Serbia, Brazil and now the US, has shown the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises and could, perhaps, begin the reversal of a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism. The US vote could even shake Europe’s ailing mainstream parties out of their fatalistic mimicking of far-right policies and into action. Gen Z voters fuelled the US blue wave , which showed a yearning for generational change. At a time when youth-led protest movements have rocked Europe, progressive parties may be able to channel protest energy into serious political change. They can’t say they haven’t been warned, loudly, to heed calls for democratic renewal, education, decent housing , equality and limits on the power of the big tech billionaires. Or that failure to do so could allow grassroots anger to be co-opted into the same kind of anti-system nihilism that fuelled Maga.
